content: Recent advancements in HIV testing have significantly improved global coverage, with over half of all individuals living with HIV now aware of their status. Early detection of chronic hepatitis B (HBV) or hepatitis C (HCV) infections is critical, as it allows affected individuals to access timely care and treatment, which can prevent or delay the progression of liver disease. Additionally, early identification can help prevent transmission through measures such as HBV vaccination for non-immune household contacts and sexual partners. The low rates of hepatitis testing in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) are attributed to several factors. These include limited availability of testing facilities and services, the absence of effective national testing policies or standards due to weak or non-existent hepatitis surveillance programs, and the high cost and complexity of diagnostic assays and algorithms. Other barriers include inadequate laboratory infrastructure, poor-quality test kits and reagents, and the unaffordability of HBV and HCV treatments for those most in need, even when diagnosed. Testing and diagnosis of HBV and HCV infections serve as the gateway to prevention, care, and treatment services. The primary goals of testing are to identify infected individuals and link them, along with their partners and families, to appropriate care and treatment services. This reduces hepatitis-related mortality by providing direct-acting curative antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis C and lifelong antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B. Testing also facilitates preventive interventions, such as HBV vaccination and the implementation of measures to reduce further transmission. Additionally, testing is essential for monitoring the response to antiviral treatment. Hepatitis testing is also conducted for other purposes, such as surveillance of acute and chronic hepatitis to detect outbreaks, monitor incidence trends, and identify risk factors for new infections. Screening by blood transfusion services is another critical application, ensuring that blood donations at risk of transmitting infections are excluded. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized viral hepatitis as a global public health problem and has developed comprehensive strategies to address it. However, previous WHO guidelines on HBV and HCV treatment did not provide detailed guidance on who to test and how to test for diagnosis. The Global Health Sector Strategy on Viral Hepatitis (2016–2021) is the first global strategy addressing viral hepatitis and aims to reduce the global burden of HBV and HCV infections, particularly in LMICs where the disease burden is highest. The WHO guidelines on hepatitis testing aim to provide evidence-based recommendations on screening for HBV and HCV infections, testing strategies, and algorithms. They also offer implementation guidance to support operationalization at the country level, including assay selection, quality systems, and planning frameworks. The guidelines emphasize the importance of promoting human rights and equity in access to hepatitis testing, ensuring that testing is accessible to the most affected populations in a stigma-free and non-discriminatory environment. Informed consent and confidentiality are fundamental principles of good clinical practice. The public health approach to hepatitis testing and treatment seeks to ensure the widest possible access to high-quality services at the population level. This approach is based on simplified and standardized methods that can be scaled up and decentralized, particularly in resource-limited settings. It aims to balance the best-proven standards of care with feasibility on a large scale, promoting health equity, gender equality, community engagement, and collaboration between public and private sectors. The WHO 5 Cs—Consent, Confidentiality, Counseling, Correct test results, and Connection to care—are guiding principles for all hepatitis testing models. Testing must always be voluntary, with informed consent obtained through pre-test information. Testing should be linked to prevention, treatment, care, and support services to maximize individual and public health benefits. Mandatory or coercive testing is never appropriate, and all testing sites must ensure client confidentiality. Accurate testing is essential to identify individuals requiring treatment while avoiding inappropriate treatment for those who do not need it. This requires reliable, high-quality, regulatory-approved test kits, qualified and trained personnel, and a quality-assured testing environment. Countries must plan their approach to implementing quality hepatitis testing services, considering local epidemiology, laboratory capacity, and available resources. The WHO guidelines were developed with input from a diverse group of stakeholders, including researchers, clinicians, program managers, and advocacy groups. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were conducted to evaluate diagnostic performance and testing strategies, although evidence for patient-important outcomes remains limited. Additional work, such as cost-effectiveness reviews, was commissioned to support the recommendations.
